question: Why do mucous membranes absorb medicines so quickly?

options.C: A thick outer layer of dry skin
options.D: A rich network of blood vessels

explanation: Think of mucous membranes like a busy market with delivery vans parked right at the gate! They have lots of tiny blood vessels close to the surface, so drugs get picked up and carried into the bloodstream in no time.

question: When is using a mucous membrane route (like sublingual or rectal) a lifesaver for a patient?

options.A: When the patient needs a subcutaneous injection
options.B: When the medication must bypass the skin entirely
options.C: When the patient is unable to swallow oral medications
options.D: When the drug requires slow digestion in the stomach

explanation: Spot on! If a patient is too weak, drowsy, or vomiting too much to swallow pills, routes like under the tongue or rectally keep their treatment going smoothly.

question: Where should you tell a patient to place a sublingual tablet?

options.C: Swallowed with a full glass of water

explanation: You've got it! 'Sub' means under, and 'lingual' means tongue. Slipping it right there lets it melt away and soak straight into the blood vessels.

question: Why shouldn't patients chew or swallow sublingual or buccal medications right away?

options.A: The medication will instantly crystallize in the stomach
options.B: Swallowing destroys the first-pass effect protection and digestive enzymes may break down the drug
options.C: Swallowing increases the absorption speed too much
options.D: Chewing causes severe irritation to the inner cheek lining

explanation: If they swallow it like a regular pill, stomach acid and the liver (first-pass metabolism) will chew it up and weaken the drug before it even gets to work. Let it dissolve where it is!

question: Where is the safest spot to drop medicated eye drops into a patient's eye?

options.D: In the inner corner of the eye

explanation: Gently pulling down the lower lid creates a nice little pocket (the conjunctival sac). Dropping it here prevents poking the sensitive cornea and keeps the medication right where it's needed.

question: When giving ear drops to an adult, how should you pull the ear pinna?
explanation: Great clinical technique! For adults, pulling the pinna upward and backward straightens out that curvy ear canal so your drops flow smoothly down to the eardrum.

question: When inserting a rectal suppository, past which structure must it go to stay in place?
explanation: You want to push it just past that internal sphincter muscle. If you don't, the body's natural reflex will push it right back out. Good nursing touch makes all the difference!

question: Which situation makes the rectal route a great choice for your patient?

options.A: When the client has an active rectal fissure
options.B: When the client prefers oral tablets
options.C: When the client has severe diarrhea
options.D: When the client is experiencing severe vomiting

explanation: When vomiting means a patient can't keep a single pill down, the rectal route steps in as a reliable way to get systemic medications into their body.

question: What is the big pharmacokinetic perk of using sublingual and buccal routes?

options.C: Direct absorption into the lymphatic system
options.D: Destruction of the drug in the stomach

explanation: By soaking directly into the blood vessels in the mouth, the drug skips the trip through the liver, meaning more active medicine reaches the rest of the body intact!

question: What physical property helps a drug cross a mucous membrane in a hurry?
explanation: Like dissolves like! Because cell membranes are made of fats (lipids), fat-loving (lipid-soluble) drugs slip right through them with ease.

question: What is one common drawback of giving medications through mucous membranes?

options.B: Longer time to onset than oral tablets
options.C: Risk of local irritation and variable absorption
options.D: Elimination of the need for nurse verification

explanation: Tissues in the mouth, rectum, or eyes can sometimes get sore or irritated by potent drugs, and how fast they absorb can change depending on how moist or healthy the tissue is.

question: Which of these is NOT a perk of using mucous membrane drug routes?

options.C: Slowest possible onset of drug action

explanation: Quite the opposite! Because mucous membranes are packed with blood vessels, they usually give a very fast onset of action, not a slow one.

question: What should you tell a patient taking a sublingual medication?

options.A: Brush your teeth immediately before placing the tablet
options.B: Chew the tablet thoroughly and swallow with a large glass of water
options.C: Do not eat or drink until the tablet has completely dissolved
options.D: Swallow the tablet whole right after placement

explanation: Remind your patient to be patient! Eating, drinking, or talking can wash the pill away before it has a chance to soak into the mucous membranes.

question: What is a crucial check a nurse must do before giving any mucous membrane medication?

options.A: Instruct the patient to hold their breath for two minutes
options.B: Apply a thick layer of petroleum jelly over the site
options.C: Crush the medication to speed up local absorption
options.D: Inspect the target membrane for irritation or lesions

explanation: Always take a quick look first! Checking the tissue ensures there are no open sores or heavy irritation that could make absorption painful or unsafe for the patient.
